subject: 반사실적 조건문은 무엇을 말하는가
title: What we mean when we say it would have been otherwise
content: Counterfactual claims appear constantly in ordinary speech and in careful philosophical argument alike. Had the match been struck, it would have lit; had the driver braked, the child would have lived. These statements seem simple enough, yet their truth remains puzzling, because they describe events that never actually happened. The match was never struck, therefore no such event exists, and no observation settles whether the claim holds. A genuine philosophical problem emerges at once: how can any statement be true when whatever it describes never occurred? One familiar answer denies that these claims describe events at all. Instead they express regular patterns, and patterns are among the things knowledge properly concerns. Saying that the match would have lit amounts to saying that dry matches light whenever struck, together with the truth that this match was dry. Although the reading has obvious appeal, it carries a matching cost, because it makes such judgments depend upon regularities nobody has confirmed. Another approach invites us to imagine matters altered as little as possible. Earlier conditions remain fixed, a single element changes, and everything else follows accordingly. The match is struck, the surroundings stay unchanged, and within that neighbouring situation it lights. On this reading the claim is true provided the nearest such situation agrees with it. Although the picture is vivid, it raises a hard question of its own: what makes one situation closer to ours than another? Any answer must rely upon a judgment about relevance, and relevance is never supplied by observation alone. Both accounts nevertheless meet in a single insight of real moral weight. Reasoning about unrealised possibilities is anything but idle, since it underlies our attributions of blame, our search for causes, and our judgments about the rightness of decisions. Whenever we ask whether a fire would have spread without the accompanying wind, we are investigating exactly what the wind accomplished. Our whole grasp of causation, and much of our moral practice, depends upon this strange but indispensable habit.

subject: 실험의 재현 가능성과 지식
title: Why a result must be seen twice
content: A single result establishes remarkably little, whatever its apparent strength. Any individual trial may succeed through luck, or through a defect nobody involved detected, and therefore a claim earns acceptance only when independent workers obtain the same outcome again. This demand for repetition is not a minor rule of laboratory practice. It belongs to the philosophical question of what knowledge amounts to, because a truth that only one group can reach resembles an accident more than a genuine finding. Yet the demand proves harder to satisfy than it initially sounds. When a second team repeats a study, it never repeats it exactly. The room differs, the season differs, and the participants differ. Consequently the team must judge which of these variations could matter, and that judgment is never delivered by the data themselves. If the fresh trial fails, one side may conclude that the original claim was false, whereas the other may argue that the copy was careless. Nothing within the numbers settles which reading deserves acceptance. This gap explains why failed repetitions rarely end a dispute outright. They redistribute the burden of argument, although they leave room for a defender to identify some hidden difference. Such moves are sometimes mere excuses, yet occasionally they are correct, because genuine effects do depend on conditions nobody thought worth recording. The honest response is to state those conditions openly beforehand. What emerges is a picture of knowledge assembled slowly by many hands. No trial is final, and no single group holds the last word. A claim grows firm as it survives repeated attempts in different places, and it weakens as those attempts fall short. Because the whole process is public, its authority rests less upon any single ingenious study than upon a shared habit of checking. Knowledge established this way never achieves certainty, and yet it remains far sturdier than any private conviction, however confident, could ever manage to become.

subject: 분류는 발견인가 결정인가
title: Whether our kinds are found or made
content: Every discipline sorts the world into kinds, and each such grouping performs genuine work. Chemists speak of metals, physicians of diseases, and lawyers of persons. Yet a hard philosophical question underlies all of them. When we assign two things to one class, are we recording a boundary that already existed, or are we drawing that boundary ourselves? The first answer holds that nature arrives already jointed, and that a good scheme cuts at those joints. Gold is one substance and lead another, therefore no decision of ours could make them exchange places. This view carries obvious force wherever the classes seem to lie waiting for discovery. It fits other cases badly, however. Consider how we group living things, or how we mark the boundaries of an illness. Here the properties vary by degree, they blend at the margins, and any division will strand difficult examples on both sides. Consequently some argue that our kinds are instruments rather than discoveries. We group things in whatever manner serves our purposes, and a scheme counts as good if it helps us predict, treat, or explain. Although this makes the world appear soft, it need not, because an instrument can fail, and a poor scheme fails conspicuously. Perhaps the two answers stand less opposed than they initially appear. Our purposes determine which properties we attend to, whereas nature determines whether things so grouped will actually behave alike. We choose to sort by weight rather than by colour; the world then reveals whether weight predicts anything valuable. On this reading a class is neither pure discovery nor pure decision, since it marks the meeting of an interest with a pattern. That meeting carries considerable moral and philosophical weight beyond the laboratory, since questions of value intrude wherever classification touches persons. Whenever a trait is classified as a disorder, or a population is classified by race, the classification alters how people are treated and how they understand themselves. Such kinds partly shape the very things they claim merely to describe.

subject: 최선의 설명으로의 추론
title: Believing the explanation that fits best
content: Much of what we count as knowledge was never directly observed. We infer it from traces, and the principle we employ is easily stated: among the explanations that would account for our evidence, believe whichever accounts for it best. A physician reasons this way from a rash, a judge from a pattern of testimony, and a researcher from a mark upon a plate. Because the principle is so common, it becomes easy to overlook how much it quietly assumes. Its first assumption is that competing explanations can be ranked at all. We call one better if it is simpler, if it leaves less unexplained, or if it agrees with what we already believe. Yet these standards can pull apart. A simple account may strain against established truths, whereas a rich account may accommodate everything by adding elements nobody can check. Therefore the ranking demands a judgment of value, and reasonable people equally committed to truth may rank identical evidence differently. A deeper worry follows immediately. Even the strongest explanation on our list may be poor, since the list contains only what somebody managed to imagine. If the correct account never occurred to anyone, we shall still crown a winner, and we shall believe it with undiminished warmth. This danger is genuine in any field where the range of possible causes is wide. Although the risk is plain, we cannot escape it by refusing to infer, because waiting for certainty would leave us knowing almost nothing. What remains available is proportion. We can hold such beliefs with a grip matching their actual support, deliberately seek rival explanations rather than settling for whichever arrived first, and look for the observation that would separate them. When an explanation survives that philosophical effort, our confidence has been earned, and the resulting belief holds a genuine claim upon truth. When it has never faced a serious rival, our confidence rests less upon the evidence than upon the poverty of our own imagination, and intellectual honesty requires admitting exactly that.

subject: 관찰 불가능한 것에 대한 믿음
title: Trusting in things no eye can see
content: Science speaks freely about things nobody has observed or could observe. Atoms, fields, genes, and forces perform heavy explanatory work, and yet none of them presents itself to the unaided eye. This raises a philosophical question that has troubled thinkers for generations. Should we believe that such things genuinely exist, or should we treat talk of them as a convenient way of speaking about what we actually measure? One side argues for belief. The theories employing these hidden entities succeed far too impressively to count as mere convenience, because they allow us to predict fresh results, build working instruments, and correct earlier mistakes. If atoms were only a manner of speaking, the success of the entire enterprise would amount to a standing miracle. Therefore the honest reading is the straightforward one: the entities are real. The opposing side proceeds more cautiously. It observes that earlier theories also succeeded, and that many of them named entities we now firmly deny. Heat was once a subtle fluid, and light once required a medium to carry it. Those accounts yielded excellent predictions in their day, so predictive success alone cannot establish that a named entity exists. Although modern cases feel considerably firmer, our predecessors felt precisely the same confidence about theirs. A middle position draws a boundary inside each theory. Certain elements genuinely drive its predictions, whereas others amount to loose decoration that could be exchanged without any loss. We may reasonably trust the working elements more than the remainder, since those alone carry the evidential weight. The suggestion is attractive, yet applying it is difficult, because the boundary usually becomes visible only long afterwards. What survives from this philosophical argument is a moral lesson about degree and intellectual honesty. Believing in unobservable things is neither foolish nor free of cost. Such belief is earned piece by piece, and it should rest more lightly upon whatever no observation has ever genuinely touched.

subject: 전문 지식과 민주적 심의
title: The expert and the public choice
content: Modern decisions rest upon knowledge that comparatively few people hold. A ruling about a medicine, a bridge, or a river depends on training that required years to acquire, and no citizen can master all of it. Yet these decisions bind everyone, and in a free society the people are supposed to govern themselves. Therefore a genuine tension runs through public life: those who know most are few, whereas those who must live with the outcome are many. One response awards the decision to the expert. If the aim is reaching the correct answer, why not entrust it to whoever can? But this answer moves too quickly. Most such questions combine two components, and only one of them is technical. How rapidly a disease spreads is a matter of fact; how much freedom to exchange for safety is a matter of value. The expert holds no special authority over the second, although training may tempt them to present their own values as findings. The opposite response awards everything to the vote. This fails equally, because a public that ignores established knowledge will choose means incapable of reaching its own ends. A decision taken against the evidence is not thereby freer; it is merely likelier to fail. Between these positions lies the harder work of joining them. The expert supplies a map of what each path would cost and yield, stating plainly wherever that map remains thin. The public supplies the purpose, deciding which costs it will accept and for whose benefit. Such a division proves easier to describe than to maintain, since experts must judge what deserves presenting and citizens must judge whom to trust. Trust is the hinge, and genuine trust is never blind. It accumulates when advice is candid about its own limits, when errors are acknowledged rather than concealed, and when advisers gain nothing from the particular answer they recommend. Where that trust collapses, neither knowledge nor voting can hold the arrangement together.

subject: 예방 원칙은 정당한가
title: Acting before the harm is proved
content: Certain harms cannot be undone. A species lost, a climate shifted, or a soil poisoned will not return merely because we later recognise our error, and this plain truth has led many to defend caution as a moral principle. On such a view we ought to prevent a grave harm before conclusive proof arrives, since waiting for proof may mean waiting until the harm is permanent. The argument carries genuine force wherever three conditions hold together. The harm must be severe, it must resist reversal, and the evidence must be real although short of certainty. Under those conditions the ordinary demand for proof functions badly, because it places the entire weight of doubt upon whoever would suffer. Therefore shifting that weight is not a retreat from rational argument; it is a moral decision about who bears the risk of error. Yet the principle is easily stated and awkwardly bounded. Almost any action might conceivably produce some grave harm, and consequently a strict reading would forbid everything, including the caution it recommends. Delay is itself an action carrying costs, and a medicine withheld or a harvest refused can kill as surely as one released prematurely. Although these costs remain less visible, they are no less genuine. A workable version of the principle therefore demands considerably more than fear. It demands a stated pathway by which the harm would arrive, evidence that the pathway is genuinely open, and a remedy proportioned to whatever is feared. It further demands that the remedy be reconsidered as knowledge accumulates, rather than left standing through mere habit. Understood this way, caution grants nobody a licence to obstruct whatever happens to be new. It is a principle about the order of proof within a narrow class of cases, and its entire justification derives from the observation that certain doors, once closed, can never afterwards be reopened by anyone.

subject: 집단 행동의 딜레마와 도덕
title: When each small share seems to weigh nothing
content: A common pasture is grazed by many herders. Each gains the full value of one additional animal, whereas the cost of the exhausted ground is distributed among them all, and therefore each finds it reasonable to add another. The pasture fails, and every herder ends worse off than before. Nothing in this account requires anybody to be greedy or stupid. It demonstrates that decisions which are sensible individually can prove ruinous collectively, and that is precisely what makes the moral problem hard. The difficulty bites hardest at the level of the single action. My one car, my one flight, or my one purchase alters the outcome by a quantity too small to measure. If the harm depends upon the total, and my share of that total approaches nothing, then apparently I commit no wrong. Yet if that argument holds for me, it holds for everyone, and consequently the harm acquires no author whatever. Therefore something within the argument must be mistaken. One reply denies that immeasurable effects are no effects. A contribution too small to detect remains a contribution, and countless such contributions are exactly what the harm consists of. Another reply reframes the question. Rather than asking what my action accomplishes, it asks which principle I could accept for everyone similarly placed, and the principle permitting each to take freely is one nobody could rationally accept. Although the replies differ, they converge upon the same verdict. A third reply looks beyond the individual actor altogether. If the trouble lies in the structure of the choice, then the remedy lies there also: change the rules, price the cost, or bind everyone simultaneously. Such measures are not an evasion of moral responsibility. They are how an obligation that no person can discharge alone actually gets discharged, and the first thing each of us owes may be support for whatever arrangement makes the remainder possible.

subject: 세금의 도덕적 근거
title: On what ground the state may take
content: A tax is a demand supported by force. The state names a sum, and whoever refuses faces the loss of property or of liberty, so any adequate account must explain why this differs from simple theft. The bare reply that the money is well spent will not serve, since a thief could offer the same defence. What is required is a moral argument addressing the taking itself. One traditional answer treats the tax as a fee. We enjoy roads, courts, and security, and justice apparently requires that those who share such goods should share their cost. This carries real force, although it strains at the edges, because we never requested these goods and cannot decline them. A fee nobody may refuse is a peculiar sort of fee. A second answer begins considerably further back. It denies that any pre-tax income exists to be taken. Whatever a person earns depends upon rules of property, contract, and exchange that only a state can sustain, and those rules already specify the terms on which gains are divided. On this view the question is not how much the state may take, but which set of rules is just. Although the shift appears subtle, it transforms the entire argument, since taxation now belongs to the framework rather than constituting a raid upon it. Neither answer settles the harder questions of degree. Both leave open how much should be raised, from whom, and toward which ends, and those decisions turn upon judgments about need, desert, and the value of leaving people alone. What the answers do settle is the argument's proper tone. Once we recognise that holdings depend upon shared rules, the taxpayer is not simply surrendering something already theirs. They are meeting the conditions under which anything counts as theirs whatever, and the case for or against a particular rate must be argued on exactly those terms.

subject: 노동과 자기실현
title: Whether work can make a person whole
content: Through most of recorded history labour counted as a burden to be endured, and the good life was thought to lie elsewhere entirely. Yet a powerful strand of modern moral thought claims the reverse: that in working we partly create ourselves, and that a person severed from meaningful work is severed from something essential. The claim deserves serious argument, because it shapes how we judge a job to be good or bad. The philosophical case rests upon a straightforward moral truth concerning making. Whenever I produce something, my purpose acquires a definite form outside me, and I can recognise within the result whatever I intended and however well I achieved it. Such work engages my judgment, instructs me through its failures, and connects me with whoever uses what I made. Therefore meaningful labour is not merely a method of earning money. It is among the few arenas where a person acts upon the world at a scale they can genuinely grasp. But the identical account explains why so much contemporary employment fails this demanding test. If a task is divided into fragments too small to carry a purpose, if the worker controls neither the pace nor the aim, and if the product vanishes into a stream nobody can follow, then the work returns nothing. It consumes considerable time and yields wages, and although wages obviously matter, they cannot supply whatever this argument identifies as valuable. A serious objection cuts against this entire philosophical picture. Claiming that work makes us whole can become a demand that people locate their meaning within a job, and that demand serves employers admirably. It can shame those whose labour is dull through no fault of their own, and it can excuse miserable pay by renaming the task a calling. The safer version of the moral claim is considerably more modest. Good work is one path toward a full life rather than the only path, and the proper aim of public value is widening that path rather than praising whoever already walks along it.

subject: 경쟁은 공정할 수 있는가
title: What a fair contest would require
content: We settle a great deal by competition. Places at a school, positions, and prizes go to whoever performs best, and we accept the outcome because the rule appears just: identical conditions for everyone, with the strongest performance winning. Yet the more closely one examines actual contests, the harder it becomes to claim that this ideal has ever been realised. Consider what genuine fairness would demand. Everyone competing must begin from the same line, they must have enjoyed the same opportunity to prepare, and the course must not reward one particular style. In a footrace we can approach these conditions. In the contests deciding a life we cannot, because preparation began at birth and was financed by parents, and the course was designed by people who had already run it. Therefore the winner's performance reflects the starting point quite as much as the effort. One response insists that only the contest itself must be fair, and that whatever preceded it belongs to another question. But this separates the competition from its own justification, and justice requires that a reward correspond to something the winner actually did. We reward the winner because we read the result as evidence about them, and if the result mainly records where they began, the reward has lost its moral ground. Although the test may be administered impeccably, the outcome is not thereby deserved. A second response accepts the flaw and works upon the starting line. It invests in the years before the contest, so that the line approaches truth. This is the honest path, yet it never finishes, since differences of family, health, and luck cannot be levelled away entirely. Perhaps the wisest conclusion is that fairness in competition admits of degree, and that our confidence in results should track it. Where the starting line is grossly uneven, victory tells us little about desert. It tells us who was positioned to win, and treating it as anything more converts an accident of birth into a claim of merit.

subject: 교육의 목적은 무엇인가
title: What schools are for
content: Ask what a school exists for and answers arrive quickly, yet they do not agree. Some argue it should prepare the young for employment, since a person unable to earn is hardly free. Others argue it should form citizens capable of judging public matters. Others insist it should open minds to whatever is worth knowing for its own sake, whether or not the knowledge ever pays. These purposes are not simply added together, because each shapes the ordinary day differently. If the purpose is employment, the sensible course teaches whatever the market currently wants, and tests for exactly that. This appeals obviously to whoever pays, although it contains a serious flaw. Market demands shift considerably faster than a childhood lasts, so training designed around today's positions may fit none of tomorrow's. Therefore even a narrow purpose points back toward broader powers of thought. If the purpose is citizenship, the school must attempt something schools find awkward. It must allow the young to argue about matters on which their elders genuinely differ, and it must teach them to weigh a claim rather than absorb it. Although this is risky, a state unwilling to accept the risk must depend upon habit instead of judgment, and habit fails whenever the situation is novel. The third purpose, knowledge pursued for its own value, is easiest to ridicule and hardest to abandon. It answers a question the others cannot: why any of this should matter to the person sitting in the room. A life shaped entirely by usefulness is a thin life, and the schooling years are among the few in which somebody may examine something simply because it exists. Perhaps these purposes quarrel less than they appear. Each requires a mind that can read closely, follow an argument, and change upon evidence. Those powers serve the worker, the citizen, and the person alike, and no school failing to build them has served any of the three.

subject: 노년과 자율의 축소
title: When the power to choose grows small
content: We treat self government as a fundamental value. An adult decides where to live, what to risk, and how to spend a day, and overriding such choices is morally serious. Yet late in life this power frequently narrows, not through any single act of force, but through gradual steps that each appear kind. A staircase becomes difficult, therefore a bedroom is relocated downstairs. Memory falters, therefore financial matters are transferred to somebody else. Each individual step appears small, although together they can leave a person inhabiting a life entirely chosen by other people. The moral difficulty is that these steps are ordinarily taken in complete good faith. Whoever takes them perceives a risk and acts to reduce it, and they are frequently correct about the risk. Therefore the question is not whether care conflicts with freedom, since it plainly can, but how the conflict should be settled and by whom. Any rule invariably favouring safety will strip a life of everything that originally made it worth having. Any rule invariably favouring choice will stand aside while somebody comes to serious harm. One useful approach asks whatever the person themselves would genuinely value. Some would rather fall at home than remain perfectly safe within a ward, and they declared exactly this long before the question arose. Although such wishes can be painful to honour, they carry the same moral authority as any other adult decision, and setting them aside because the chooser is elderly is a plain error of justice. A second move protects the small choices even where the large ones must go. Somebody who can no longer manage a household may still decide when to rise, what to wear, and whom to receive. These may resemble trifles beside questions of money and housing, but they constitute the texture of a day, and they are where the sense of remaining oneself survives. Leaving them in a person's hands costs almost nothing, whereas removing them inflicts a loss that no additional safety repays.

subject: 우정의 도덕적 요구
title: What a friend may rightly ask
content: Morality is often taught as a matter of treating everyone alike. We should not favour one person over another, and a principle that would not hold for a stranger should hold for nobody. Yet friendship appears to operate otherwise. A friend is precisely the person for whom we do more, whose call we answer at any hour, and whose troubles weigh upon us as another's would not. This looks like partiality, and partiality is exactly what justice seems to forbid. One escape claims that friendship falls outside the moral field altogether, belonging to private taste. But this cannot hold, because friendship generates demands that function like obligations. If a friend needs help and I fail to come, I have not merely disappointed them; I have failed at something, and we both recognise it. Therefore these bonds carry moral weight, and the problem cannot be avoided by calling them personal. A better answer notices what the demand for equal treatment was ever meant to govern. It governs how we exercise power over others, how we distribute what is held in common, and how we judge people we do not know. It was never meant to abolish close attachments, since a world where nobody mattered specially to anybody would be poorer in every important respect. Although we owe strangers a great deal, we do not owe them whatever we owe a friend. The genuinely hard cases arise where the two claims meet. A friend may ask me to lie for them, to overlook a wrong, or to hand them something owed to somebody else, and here the bond has reached its moral limit. What a friend may rightly ask is help that costs me, not help that costs a third party who never agreed to bear it. A friendship demanding such wrongs is not a deeper loyalty; it is a demand that one of us abandon being a decent person.

subject: 용기와 무모함의 구분
title: The line between brave and rash
content: Courage is praised in every age, and yet it is remarkably easy to praise the wrong thing. Somebody running into a burning house and somebody driving at speed for excitement both confront danger, and both may feel the identical rush. Therefore we need a way of distinguishing them, and the difference cannot lie in the quantity of risk alone, since the reckless frequently risk less than the brave. An ancient moral philosophy places this virtue between two failings, treating courage as a mean between opposed vices. On one side stands the coward, who flees whatever should be faced. On the other stands the reckless person, who charges at whatever should be avoided. Courage is neither, and its mark is that the fear somebody feels matches the danger actually present. The brave are not without fear; they feel it in the right measure and act well regardless. The account is valuable because it directs attention toward judgment rather than nerve. Acting well under threat requires reading the threat correctly, weighing whatever may be lost against whatever may be saved, and knowing one's own powers. Although the reckless person may display tremendous nerve, they have skipped this reading, and consequently their nerve is worth nothing to whoever they meant to help. A second mark concerns the purpose. Courage is displayed in service of something worth the danger, whether a person, an obligation, or a truth that must be spoken. Remove the purpose and the identical action becomes mere display. This explains why we never call a bully brave, although bullies frequently face genuine risk. The two marks operate together. Sound judgment without a worthy purpose amounts only to prudence, whereas a worthy purpose without judgment is how admirable people get killed for nothing. What we genuinely admire as moral virtue is the union of both, and that union is rarer, and considerably more valuable, than any raw willingness to face harm.

subject: 분노의 도덕적 기능
title: Whether anger has a place in a good life
content: Anger enjoys a poor reputation among moral teachers. It clouds thought, it feeds upon itself, and it has driven more cruelty than any other passion, so a long tradition has urged us to eliminate it entirely. Yet the argument against it is less clean than it appears, because anger is not merely a heat in the blood. It carries a moral judgment, and that judgment is frequently true. When I am angry at a wrong, I am perceiving something real. I perceive that a person was treated as though they did not count, and my anger is the form that perception takes. Therefore somebody who felt nothing at such treatment would not be calm and wise; they would be missing something morally important. This is clearest where the injured party is oneself. Anger is how a person registers that they were owed better, and those trained out of it become easy to exploit. The danger lies in whatever anger wants next. Alongside the accurate judgment there frequently rides a wish for the wrongdoer to suffer, and that wish benefits nobody. It will not undo the harm, it tends to grow beyond any measure, and it binds the angry person to the worst hour of their life. Although the first component of anger sees clearly, this second component sees nothing whatever. A useful moral path preserves the judgment about justice and discards the wish for suffering. One can maintain that a wrong occurred, say so plainly, and press for justice, without desiring the pain of whoever caused it. Such a stance is not meekness, since it makes a firmer demand than rage ever manages. It is also difficult, and nobody holds it steadily. What it offers is a way of taking wrongs seriously without being governed by them, and that may be the most that can reasonably be asked of a feeling we never chose to have.

subject: 자기 존중의 근거
title: The ground on which we stand
content: Self respect is not identical with thinking well of oneself. A person may be proud of their talents and still lack it, whereas another may know their faults in detail and possess it entirely, so the two must rest upon different foundations. Pride examines whatever one has accomplished. Self respect examines whatever one is owed, and it reveals itself in what a person will refuse. Where does such a stance originate? One answer grounds it in achievement. We respect ourselves because we have met a standard, kept a promise, or produced work we can defend, and this is not empty, since a life of broken undertakings genuinely wears somebody down. But the answer cannot be the entire story. If self respect rose and fell with success, then the sick, the failing, and the elderly would forfeit their claim upon it, and that conclusion deserves rejection rather than acceptance. Therefore a second foundation is required, one independent of the record. It lies in standing as a person among persons, holding the same claim to be heard and counted as anybody else. On this footing self respect is not a verdict about oneself whatever. It is a grasp of one's moral position, and it remains available to somebody who has failed at everything they attempted. What follows is practical. A person holding this grasp does not beg for whatever is rightfully theirs, does not accept contempt as the price of assistance, and does not measure their value by another's approval. Although they may be humble about their gifts, they are not humble about their standing, and these are entirely different things. This also imposes a demand upon everyone else. Self respect is difficult to sustain alone, since it is fed or starved by how one is treated. A society that addresses some of its members as though they were burdens should not be surprised when they eventually believe it.

subject: 삶의 의미를 묻는다는 것
title: What the question about meaning asks
content: People ask what their life means, ordinarily at a difficult hour, and the philosophical question resists any simple answer. Part of the trouble is that it constitutes several questions rather than one, and they require entirely different replies. Sorting them settles nothing by itself, yet it clears away a considerable quantity of needless despair. One reading enquires after a moral purpose established from outside the person. On this view a life has meaning if it plays a part within some larger design, and if no such design exists then nothing means anything. But this reading produces a distinctly odd result. If a purpose were handed to us, and we found it dull or cruel, we would not accept it merely because its source was elevated. Therefore our own moral judgment is already working here, and the external source cannot supply the whole ground. A second philosophical reading turns inward instead. A life has meaning if whoever lives it finds it worth living, and nothing further is required. This comes considerably closer to the truth, although taken alone it travels too far. A life spent upon something empty does not become full because the person is contented, and honestly we do not believe that it does. What seems to be wanted is a meeting between these two accounts. A life goes well in this respect when a person cares about something genuinely worth caring about, and gives themselves to it over time. The caring must be real, therefore it cannot be assigned; the object must have value, therefore it cannot be anything whatever. Neither component suffices entirely on its own. Understood this way, the question concerns a life rather than the universe. It asks whether the things one spends one's days upon will bear the weight one places upon them, and that is a question a person can actually work with. It admits of better and worse answers, and unlike the grander version, it can be answered within the years available.

subject: 설명과 예측의 비대칭
title: Why the two do not run both ways
content: It is tempting to assume that explaining and predicting amount to one activity viewed from opposite sides. If I can say why something happened, then presumably I could have said beforehand that it would; and if I can foretell an event, then presumably I can explain why it arrives. This tidy picture has an ancient pedigree, and it is mistaken in both directions. Consider the second half first. A falling glass will break, and I can announce this before it lands, but the fact that I can foretell the outcome does not mean I have explained it. A sailor may predict a storm from the ache of an old wound, yet the ache does not produce the storm. Therefore a reliable sign is not a cause, and prediction can operate upon signs alone. The first half fails just as plainly. We explain the shape of a species by the pressures it encountered, and we explain a collapse by the strains that accumulated, but neither account would have permitted us to name the outcome beforehand. The reason is that such systems are open. Small differences early on grow large, and the relevant factors exceed counting, so we can trace a pathway backward that we could never have drawn forward. What separates the two activities is direction and detail. Explaining fits an event into a pattern of causes after we know it occurred, which permits us to ignore every pathway not taken. Predicting selects one pathway from many while all of them remain open, and that demands considerably more. Although identical laws serve both tasks, the burden is not identical. This matters whenever we judge a discipline by its forecasts. Geology, medicine, and history explain a great deal and foretell rather little, and the gap is not invariably a symptom of weakness. It can be a truth about the subject rather than a fault in whoever studies it.

subject: 이론 간 통약 불가능성
title: When two accounts cannot be laid side by side
content: We prefer to assume that theories can be compared. Place them beside each other, determine which explains more, and choose accordingly. Yet some philosophers have argued that rival accounts can differ so profoundly that no common measure exists, and that the choice between them is never settled by evidence alone. The claim sounds extreme, although the philosophical argument behind it repays careful attention, since it concerns how knowledge itself changes. Its first ground is that words shift their sense. When one account replaces another, the older terms may survive while their meaning quietly changes underneath. Mass within one scheme is not quite mass within the next, and consequently a claim that appears to be denied is not the identical claim. Therefore a direct conflict may be an illusion, since the two sides are not invariably discussing one thing. A second ground concerns what counts as evidence. Each account brings its own sense of which questions matter and which results are telling, and a fact that one side treats as central may be dismissed by the other as a detail. If the two disagree about the scoreboard, they cannot settle the match by playing. Although the picture carries genuine force, it is frequently pushed too far. Rival accounts rarely fail to touch at any point whatever. They share instruments, they must both accommodate whatever those instruments display, and their supporters do argue and occasionally change their minds. A gap in shared meaning renders comparison difficult rather than impossible, and translation between them, while never exact, is ordinarily adequate. What survives is a warning about how such choices actually happen. Changing theories is not a simple arithmetic in which one column defeats another. It involves learning to perceive a field differently, and that requires time, argument, and a generation willing to attempt it. Progress toward truth is genuine, yet it is slower and considerably messier than the tidy story of weighing evidence would suggest.

subject: 불확실성 아래의 의무
title: Doing right when the facts are unclear
content: Most moral advice assumes that we know what we are doing. Avoid harm, keep your promises, help whoever is in need: each principle applies easily once the facts are established. Yet in actual decisions the facts are rarely established. We act upon estimates about whatever will follow, and those estimates may be wrong, so a question arises that the principles never answer. What does a person owe when the outcome cannot be known? One view holds that obligation tracks the facts themselves. If an action would genuinely cause harm, it was wrong, whatever the agent believed. This carries a hard appeal, because it keeps morality anchored to the world rather than to opinion. But it produces a strange result. It implies that a careful person who took every reasonable precaution may still have acted wrongly through sheer misfortune, and that nobody could ever know at the time what they ought to do. A second view ties obligation to the available evidence. On this reading a person acts rightly if they weigh whatever they can know and choose well by that light, even where the result is terrible. Although this is kinder, it can slide into excuse, since anybody can claim they did not know. Therefore the view requires a further demand: that one must also take reasonable steps toward finding out. The two views may be answering different questions. One asks which action would have been best, which we can judge only afterwards; the other asks what this person should have done, which is exactly what they needed at the time. Both are genuine, and confusing them generates much fruitless argument. What follows for practice is modest but useful. Gather whatever evidence the stakes deserve, weigh harms by their likelihood and gravity, prefer the path you could defend to somebody bearing the risk, and accept that even excellent judgment sometimes ends badly.

subject: 여가의 가치
title: Why free time is more than rest
content: We describe free time as a pause from work, a space for recovery so that we may work again afterwards. This formulation makes leisure a servant of labour, and it suits an age that measures a day by whatever it produced. Yet an older moral tradition held the reverse. It treated free time as the entire point of the arrangement, and work as the price we pay to secure it. The older view rests upon a simple thought. Some things are done for the sake of something else, whereas others are done for their own sake, and a life must contain the second kind or it possesses no end whatever. Play, friendship, study, and the making of things nobody requested belong to that second kind. Therefore they are not gaps within a life; they are whatever the remainder exists for. Two habits obscure this. The first converts free time into another task, filled with targets and measured for gain, so that even rest must be productive. The second converts it into mere idleness, in which hours pass leaving nothing behind. Although these appear opposite, they share a failure to take the time seriously, since neither treats it as a space where a person chooses what they genuinely value. A further point is political. Free time is not distributed evenly. Those working long hours for meagre pay, and those caring for others without relief, possess very little of it, and instructing them to use their leisure well approaches mockery. A society valuing such time must arrange for people to have some, through hours, pay, and shared care. What is at stake is not comfort but freedom, and therefore a question of justice. It is whether people hold any portion of their lives that genuinely belongs to them, within which they may pursue whatever they judge worth pursuing. A life lacking that portion may be busy and even prosperous, and it will still be a life lived upon somebody else's terms.

subject: 돌봄 노동의 도덕적 지위
title: The work that holds a life together
content: Every person begins helpless and most conclude that way. Between those points lie years of illness, injury, and ordinary need, and throughout all of it somebody feeds, washes, watches, and comforts. This labour is the ground upon which every other activity stands, yet it has long been treated as though it were not labour whatever. Part of the reason is that it fell mainly upon women, and was counted as a natural expression of love rather than as work. Therefore it was omitted from the accounts, unpaid at home and poorly paid outside it. Where it is paid, the rate is low, and the justification offered is that the skill is common. But the skill is not common. Reading a need that has never been spoken, sustaining patience through a terrible night, and preserving a person's dignity while performing whatever dignity would rather conceal: these are difficult, and performing them badly leaves lasting marks. A moral tradition constructed around independent adults bargaining with one another has trouble perceiving this. Its picture begins too late, with people already grown, already fed, already able to speak for themselves. Although that picture serves adequately for questions of exchange and law, it conceals the truth that nobody arrives at the table without years of another's labour behind them. A more honest starting point treats dependence as normal rather than as a lapse. On such a view the question is not how the strong should treat the weak, since everyone is both in turn. It is how a society should distribute the burden of care so that it does not fall by accident upon whoever is least able to refuse. The answers are practical, although the argument is one of justice: paid leave, decent wages for whoever performs it, and time counted as work rather than as devotion. Each of these states the same moral truth differently, namely that this labour is real and that we all live upon it.

subject: 수치와 죄책의 차이
title: Feeling bad about the deed and about oneself
content: Two feelings follow a wrong, and although they frequently arrive together they are not identical. In the first, attention fixes upon whatever was done. I broke a promise, the thought of it presses upon me, and what I want is to repair the damage. In the second, attention fixes upon what I am. I stand exposed, I appear small, and what I want is to disappear. The first is guilt and the second is shame, and the moral difference between them shapes whatever happens next. Guilt possesses a natural path forward. Because it points at an action, it can be answered by an action: an apology, a repair, a change in behaviour. The debt is genuine but bounded, and once discharged the feeling has completed its work and may fade. Therefore guilt, however painful, tends to leave a person more able to face others rather than less. Shame moves the opposite direction. Since it points at the self rather than at any action, no particular action can settle it, and the impulse it generates is concealment. Somebody in its grip frequently avoids the very people they wronged, which renders repair harder and deepens the sense of being unfit. Although shame can push somebody toward change, it equally often pushes them toward secrecy or toward anger at whoever witnessed them. This carries practical weight in how we correct one another. Saying that an action was wrong invites the first response, whereas saying that somebody is the sort of person who does such things invites the second. Parents, teachers, and courts choose constantly between these forms, frequently without noticing. The choice is not about gentleness but about moral truth and whatever justice actually requires. A sharp charge aimed at the deed can prove far more demanding than a vague verdict upon a person, and it possesses the advantage of leaving a road back. What we usually want from a wrongdoer is repair, and only one of these feelings assists them.
